content.title: Challenges, Tipping Points and Solutions in Renewable Energy
content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations

content.text:
This lesson will present the complex challenges and transformative tipping points that will shape the future of renewable energy.

It first examines technical hurdles such as enhancing energy efficiency 💬️, ensuring grid stability, and managing cybersecurity risks in increasingly digitalized system. Then it explored the non-technical barriers like financing constraints, land and resource competition, and social acceptance.

Through evidence-based insights and forward-looking scenarios, the lesson highlights critical interventions needed to unlock solutions: from policy reforms and investment de-risking to inclusive land-use planning and community engagement.

By addressing these systemic barriers, the lesson emphasizes that a resilient, equitable, and scalable renewable energy future is possible—if proactive, coordinated action is taken today.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: A: Improving Efficiency in Renewable Energy Systems

content.text:
As renewable energy systems become an essential part of the global electricity supply, improving their efficiency is crucial to meeting rising demand while maintaining system reliability.

Between 2022 and 2030, global capacity for wind and solar PV is expected to more than double (IEA, 2024). This rapid expansion risks strain existing infrastructure, hence the need for innovations in efficiency and energy storage 💬️.


Energy efficiency has already proven to be an important lever to accelerate the deployment of renewables. From 2000 to 2023, energy intensity improvement accelerated from 0.8% per year from to around 1.8%, playing a key role in decoupling economic growth from energy consumption (IEA, 2024).

Going forward, global energy demand is projected to rise by 20% by 2030, but this increase could be cut in half through strong efficiency measures. Achieving this will require doubling the annual rate of energy intensity improvement from 2% to 4% (IEA, 2024).

content.quote: “Accelerating energy efficiency improvements can deliver over 70% of the projected decline in oil demand and 50% of the reduction in gas demand by 2030.”
content.author: IEA, 2024

content.text: The future gains from energy efficiency are significant.

content.title: Fist, advancing energy efficiency is essential to phasing out fossil fuels.
content.body: According to the IEA’s net zero emissions scenario for 2050, accelerating efficiency measures could account for over 70% of the projected drop in oil demand and half of the reduction in natural gas demand by 2030.

content.title: Second, energy efficiency plays a key role in cost effective energy access, especially in developing countries.
content.body: Indeed, energy efficiency serves as a key policy tool for lowering household energy costs. By 2050, household energy spending is projected to fall by 30% in advanced economies and 20% in EMDEs, compared to current policy trajectories, driven in part by efficiency measures like building retrofits.

content.title: Third, energy efficiency improvement can stimulate employment worldwide.
content.body: In the NZE Scenario, energy efficiency jobs increase by nearly 5 million by 2030—almost four times more than under current policies—driven primarily by building retrofits, with smaller gains in industry, appliances, and HVAC.

content.text:
To meet these ambitions, global investments in energy efficiency must triple from USD 660 billion in 2023 to USD 1.9 trillion by 2030. While nearly 90% of current spending is concentrated in China and advanced economies, investment in EMDEs needs to grow four to seven times. These regions face distinct needs, from expanding access to efficient housing and appliances to electrifying transport with solutions like electric motorbikes and promoting clean cooking 💬️ in sub-Saharan Africa.


To unlock the required scale of investment, governments should improve access to affordable capital for households and SMEs; leverage public funds to attract private investment; build institutional capacity; strengthen international cooperation to lower capital costs in EMDEs; and prioritize industrial financing, where just 6% of investment can yield 20% of global efficiency gains by 2030 (IEA, 2024).

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: B: Cybersecurity Risks in an Increasingly Digitalized Energy Grid

content.text:
Meeting the goals of a just energy transition 💬️ worldwide will require deploying cleaner technologies at scale.

This also involves managing new and evolving risks. The digitalization of power systems has led to new opportunities for cost-efficiency and optimization. Indeed, utilities increasingly use digital technologies to improve the management of plants, grids and business operations.

This contributed to energy security by facilitating the integration of distributed energy resources, improving the quality of supply and providing additional services to customers. But each element of the grid that becomes digitalized constitutes a new point of entry for cybercriminal organisations.


Cyberattacks in the electricity sector can disable remote control for power facilities, affect IT systems which can disrupt prepaid meters and lead to recurrent data breaches that reveal customer’s private data. Between 2020 and 2022 alone, the number of weekly cyberattacks more than doubled, with the average cost of data breach hitting a record high of USD 4.72 million in the energy sector. (IEA, 2023)

metadata.title: Average number of weekly cyberattacks per organization in selected industries, 2020-2022

content.text:
Emerging threats such as supply chain attacks, especially those targeting distributed energy resources and smart inverters, can add additional complexity. Additionally, there is currently a 3.4 million global shortage of cybersecurity across all sectors including energy, while cybersecurity salaries in the energy sector remain some of the lowest for the occupation globally (IEA, 2023)

In developing countries where the digital divide is more pronounced, communities may lack the capacity to build both the technological and human resource infrastructure needed to defend against cyber threats.

A strategic approach is needed to combine digital capacity building initiatives with clear incentives for training local cybersecurity professionals, especially within the energy sector.

According to the IEA NZE scenario, the global energy transition is expected to create up to 14 million new clean energy jobs by 2030, and cybersecurity expertise is crucial to ensure these sectors remain resilient (IEA, 2022).

Investing in local talent development through partnerships with tech organizations and academic institutions could drive long-term solutions. A collaborative approach across governments, private sectors, and international organizations can help create a sustainable and inclusive cybersecurity framework for energy infrastructures, especially in developing countries where digital infrastructure is still growing.

To energy systems and ensure the resilience of the future grid, the deployment of cybersecurity frameworks, international cooperation, and the integration of "cyber-by-design" principles into infrastructure planning are needed.


Protecting this infrastructure while enabling equitable access requires balancing technological innovation with upskilling, while ensuring cybersecurity resilience from the ground up.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: C: Cost Barriers, investment and financing constraints

content.text:
Despite growing global momentum, the financial landscape required for the clean energy transition remains very imbalanced, especially in emerging and developing economies.

Looking ahead, the disparity in financing conditions could become one of the most significant barriers to a just and inclusive energy future. To meet rising demand and align with climate goals, annual clean energy investment in these regions needs to be multiplied by four, from USD 770 billion in 2022 to USD 2.2-2.8 trillion by 2030 (IEA, 2023). Yet, over 80% of renewable energy investment between 2000 and 2020 flowed to high-income countries and China, a signal that persistent inequities remain (IEA, 2023).


One major obstacle is the high cost of capital (CoC) for renewable energy in developing countries, which is often 2 to 3 times higher than in advanced economies due to elements like perceived risks and the lack of de-risking mechanisms (IEA, 2023). This disparity contributes to increasing the levelized cost of electricity 💬️ (LCOE). These cost structures can make renewables less competitive, and in turn slow down their adoption in the future.

content.quote: ““Without a concerted effort to reduce the cost of capital, developing countries risk missing out on nearly one-third of their potential increase in electricity generation from renewables by 2050.”
content.author: Calcaterra et al., 2024

content.text:
If left unaddressed, these financial barriers risk delaying clean energy deployment, and could also allow for continued fossil fuel dependence and deepen development inequities in the future.


Modeling by Calcaterra et al. (2024) shows that without measures to reduce the CoC, high-cost regions risk missing up to 30% of their potential increase in renewable electricity generation by 2050 (Calcaterra et al., 2024).

On the other hand, a future scenario where favorable financing conditions converge with those of developed countries could reduce electricity prices in developing economies and cut energy expenditures as a share of GDP in regions such as Africa and Latin America.

If well-targeted and well managed, such solutions can have a transformative impact on the future of energy in developing countries.

In Africa alone, climate-financed de-risking and blended finance approaches could increase electricity generation from renewable energy by 43% by 2030 compared to a no-policy baseline (Briera & Lefèvre, 2024). This means that if concessional finance— the type of financial support provided at terms more favorable than those typically available in the market —is used strategically to reduce the financial risks faced by private investors, it becomes significantly more attractive to invest in clean energy projects.


The future of energy, especially in developing countries, will greatly depend on the ability to unlock affordable, long-term capital at scale.

This brief overview introduces how cost barriers and financing constraints shape the future of energy systems in the Global South. For a deeper dive into financing solutions and mechanisms, refer to Module 4 on Sustainable Energy Finance.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: D: Land constraints and social acceptance

content.text:
Beyond capital flows, renewable energy deployment is also hindered by land-related challenges. Utility-scale solar PV and wind farms generally require significantly more land per unit of electricity generated. For example, solar PV consumes 8.7-13 m2 per MWh/year, while wind energy 💬️ uses 0.3-1.3 m2, compared to just 0.1-0.2 m2 for natural gas combined cycle plants (Fritsche et al., 2017)

These disparities translate into a significant land footprint as renewables scale up globally.

In developing regions like South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa, this spatial demand intersects with high population densities, insecure land tenure, and intense competition for land between energy, agriculture, conservation, and urbanization. Solar farms in India, for instance, are projected to require between 55,000 and 125,000 km2 by 2030 to meet national targets, which represents approximately the size of Himachal Pradesh or Chhattisgarh, respectively (Kiesecker et al., 2019). If they are not adequately planned, these developments can displace communities, disrupt agricultural activity, and limit access to shared natural resources, which risk further exacerbating poverty and inequality.
Land use conflicts are especially present in rural areas where energy projects may disrupt agricultural activity or affect communal and Indigenous lands, compounding risks of poverty and social inequality.

Future energy planning must also account for the indirect environmental impacts of land use change. Large-scale solar deployment can lead to the clearing of forest , which risk undermining the climate benefits of clean energy (van de Ven et al., 2021). Without careful spatial planning and land management, these projects risk replicating the extractive models of the past.

But solutions exist to mitigate the impact of clean energy on land use. Strategies such as seeding solar parks with pasture vegetation can reduce emissions , and in some contexts (e.g., India), may even result in net carbon sequestration (van de Ven et al., 2021).


Wind energy may present a more flexible land use energy profile. While wind farms can cover large areas (1.5–2 hectares/MW), 96–99% of the land is not permanently impacted, allowing for agricultural co-use.


Looking ahead, land will become one of the defining constraints of the energy transition, particularly in developing countries where the choice between land for food, forests, or energy is not just technical, but existential.

A future proof energy system will require land-smart planning, including prioritization of rooftops, degraded lands, and deserts; co-use strategies that align with local livelihoods; and policy frameworks that integrate energy expansion with land rights and biodiversity protection.

content.intro: M8: Renewable Energy Technologies and Innovations
content.title: Case Study: Global
content.subtitle: AI for Energy Equity: Forecasting grid challenges through clean energy index

content.text:
As the urgency to mitigate climate change intensifies, the transition to clean energy must also ensure that no one is left behind. The UNDP–IBM collaboration demonstrates how frontier technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, can support climate change mitigation and adaptation while promoting just, inclusive energy transitions.

Between 2022 and 2024, UNDP partnered with IBM through the IBM Sustainability Accelerator to co-develop two digital public goods:

Electricity Access Forecasting AI Model (EAF)

Clean Energy Equity Index (CEEI)

These tools leverage artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and geospatial analytics to support just and data-driven energy transitions. Both were integrated into UNDP’s open GeoHub platform as part of the Data Futures Exchange (DFx).

These tools help governments, planners, and communities make informed, equitable decisions around clean energy investments—critical in the context of both mitigation and adaptation.

The AI-based Electricity Access Forecasting Model uses over 40 dynamic data layers—such as terrain, infrastructure, demographic trends, and environmental stressors—to obtain electricity access estimates at different geographical levels, forecast hyper-granular (1km²) estimates of electricity access from 2012 to 2030, and combine maps showing electricity access and other indicators (Geo Hub). It covers 102 countries across Africa, the Asia-Pacific region, Latin America, and the Middle East (Geo Hub).

This model enables countries to prioritize clean energy investments in regions that are both underserved and vulnerable to climate impacts. It supports mitigation by encouraging a shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources and adaptation by identifying areas where energy access is essential for resilience in key sectors, including health, agriculture, and water services.

To complement these forecasts, the Clean Energy Equity Index introduces a multidimensional equity lens to energy planning. Developed with Stony Brook University, the Clean Energy Equity Index is a district-level composite indicator (scored from 0 to 1) across 53 African countries.

It incorporates geospatial analytics and factors such as clean energy opportunities, environmental pressure (including GHG emissions), and socio-economic variables. The tool enables policymakers to identify priority areas for intervention and supports equitable, targeted clean energy transitions aligned with decarbonization 💬️ and inclusive development goals.

These tools were designed using IBM’s Garage co‑creation approach and deployed through the IBM Sustainability Accelerator. IBM contributed its watsonx AI, IBM Cloud, and Environmental Intelligence to build models that are both scalable and user‑friendly. UNDP’s contextual expertise and its national-level partnerships helped ensure relevance and adaptability. Together, the organizations created interactive, customizable models hosted on GeoHub—enhancing local capacity and transparency in energy planning.

As a result, policymakers and planners now have access to detailed, data-driven insights that can support more targeted and equitable energy investments. The tools enhance the precision and inclusiveness of decision-making by offering high-resolution, geospatially disaggregated forecasts and equity metrics. Their integration into UNDP’s GeoHub platform strengthens institutional data systems and supports long-term usability. By revealing regional disparities and making localized information publicly accessible, the tools can contribute to more informed national energy planning aligned with SDG 7 and, where relevant, climate policy frameworks such as nationally determined contributions 💬️ (NDCs) and National Adaptation Plans (NAPs).

This collaboration presents a replicable model for digital climate innovation, leveraging global technology in conjunction with development priorities to generate scalable solutions. Key lessons include the value of open-access design, cross-sector co-creation, and localized integration for success. The tools are now available to policymakers, practitioners, journalists, and the public to help build clean energy pathways that are socially just, resilient, and grounded in real-world data.

By putting data and equity at the center of clean energy transitions, the UNDP–IBM model redefines how the energy sector can respond to climate risks—proactively, fairly, and collaboratively.

This case illustrates how digital innovation can expand the frontiers of renewable energy planning, not just by deploying technology but by transforming how decisions are made. Through the use of AI, geospatial intelligence, and open-access platforms, the UNDP–IBM collaboration demonstrates how renewable energy technologies can be designed and scaled with equity, precision, and long-term adaptability at their core.

As countries seek to accelerate their clean energy transitions, tools such as the Electricity Access Forecasting Model and the Clean Energy Equity Index offer a forward-looking approach—one that merges innovation with inclusion and global expertise with local relevance. In doing so, they help redefine renewable energy not only as a solution to climate challenges but as a catalyst for more just and resilient energy systems.

takeaways.title: Energy efficiency is key for a sustainable energy future.
takeaways.description: It can reduce projected global energy demand by up to 50% by 2030 while accelerating the phase-out of fossil fuels. In addition to environmental benefits, improving efficiency lowers household energy costs and can generate millions of new jobs, especially in developing countries where access to efficient appliances and buildings remains limited

takeaways.title: Digitalization enhances energy system performance but also introduces new vulnerabilities.
takeaways.description: As grids and infrastructure become smarter and more interconnected, the risk of cyberattacks increases—posing threats to system reliability, privacy, and public trust. Addressing these challenges will require major investments in cybersecurity capacity, local skills development, and inclusive digital governance frameworks, particularly in regions with limited digital infrastructure.

takeaways.title: Overcoming non-technological barriers is essential to realizing the full potential of renewables.
takeaways.description: High capital costs, land use conflicts, and lack of public acceptance continue to hinder progress, especially in the Global South. Solutions such as concessional finance, land-smart planning, and meaningful community engagement can help ensure that renewable energy development is both equitable and sustainable.
